::: {.tut-standfirst}
The first step inside the application is loading your occurrence spreadsheet. Saíra accepts CSV, Excel and camera-trap packages, and takes care of encoding and separator detection for you.
:::

## Supported formats

| Format | Extension | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Delimited text | `.csv`, `.tsv`, `.txt` | Comma, semicolon or tab, detected automatically |
| Excel | `.xlsx`, `.xls` | You choose which sheet (tab) to import |
| Camera trap | `.zip`, `.csv` | Camtrap DP packages and Wildlife Insights exports (see below) |

Each **row** should be one occurrence (a record of an organism in a place and time) and each **column** an attribute: catalog number, species, date, locality, collector, and so on.

## Loading the file

To practice this and the next steps, download the sample spreadsheet [`ocorrencias-exemplo.csv`](../../assets/exemplo/ocorrencias-exemplo.csv), a small, deliberately imperfect dataset.

In the **Upload** tab, drag the file onto the indicated area or click to select it.

```{=html}
<ol class="steps">
  <li><strong>Select the file.</strong>
    <p>Drop the CSV, Excel or package onto the upload area.</p></li>
  <li><strong>Check the reading.</strong>
    <p>Saíra shows a preview of the first rows. Verify that the columns are split correctly and that accents look right.</p></li>
  <li><strong>Adjust encoding and separator, if needed.</strong>
    <p>If the reading came out wrong, switch the encoding or the separator in the controls and the preview updates instantly.</p></li>
  <li><strong>Pick the sheet (Excel only).</strong>
    <p>In `.xlsx`/`.xls` files with several sheets, select which tab to import.</p></li>
</ol>
```

## Automatic encoding and separator detection

When it receives a CSV, Saíra tries to guess the **encoding** (UTF-8, Latin-1/ISO-8859-1, Windows-1252) and the column **separator**, and strips the byte-order mark (BOM) that some programs add at the start of the file. It is right almost every time, but the preview exists precisely so you can confirm before moving on. Dates in various formats (`03/11/2024`, `2024-11-03`, `Nov 3 2024`) are recognized and standardized later, at export.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Accents showing up wrong?
That is almost always encoding. Brazilian spreadsheets are usually in **UTF-8** or **Latin-1 (ISO-8859-1)**. If "São Paulo" became "S&atilde;o Paulo" or "S?o Paulo", switch the encoding at import until the preview looks correct.
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
## The whole spreadsheet opened in a single column?
That is the wrong separator. Brazilian files often use a **semicolon (`;`)** because the comma is already the decimal separator. If the preview shows everything crammed into one column, switch the separator (`;`, `,` or tab) until the columns split correctly.
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
## Header on the first row
Saíra assumes the **first row** holds the column names. Remove title rows, logos or merged cells before exporting from Excel: they break the reading.
:::

## Camera-trap data

If your data comes from camera traps, Saíra recognizes the two most common formats and converts them into an occurrence table before mapping:

- **Camtrap DP** (Camera Trap Data Package): the standardized `.zip` package, with `media`, `observations` and `deployments`.
- **Wildlife Insights**: the platform's CSV export, from which Saíra derives the scientific name (from class, order, family, genus and species), the record timestamp and the observation type.

In both cases Saíra builds a consistent scientific name and organizes the time and place fields, so the rest of the workflow (mapping, names, coordinates) works just like a regular spreadsheet.

::: {.callout-note}
## Incomplete camtrap package?
If the package descriptor is missing, Saíra tries to **synthesize** one from the CSVs it finds. Even so, check in the preview that the species, date and coordinate columns came through before proceeding.
:::
